lessons.title: Values and names
lessons.body:
# Values and names

Everything Python works with is a value, and every value has a type. A name is a label that points at a value. Assignment with `=` attaches the label. It never copies anything.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a        # same list, two names
b.append(3)
print(a)     # [1, 2, 3]
a = "text"   # a now points elsewhere
print(b)     # still [1, 2, 3]
```

## Looking at a value

- `type(x).__name__` gives the name of its type.
- `repr(x)` gives an unambiguous text form, with quotes around strings.
- `None` is the value that means "nothing here".
- `==` compares values. `is` asks whether two names point at the same object, so keep it for `None`.

The right side of an assignment runs first, which is why `x, y = y, x` swaps two names without a temporary variable.

def describe(value):
    # Return "<type name>: <repr of value>"
    pass


def swap(a, b):
    # Return the two values in reverse order
    pass


# Print describe(42) here

checks.code: assert describe(3) == "int: 3", describe(3)

checks.name: strings keep their quotes
checks.code: assert describe("hi") == "str: 'hi'", describe("hi")

checks.name: None and lists have types too
checks.code:
assert describe(None) == "NoneType: None", describe(None)
assert describe([1]) == "list: [1]", describe([1])

checks.name: swap reverses a pair
checks.code:

assert swap(None, None) == (None, None), swap(None, None)

checks.code: assert "int: 42" in _stdout, _stdout

hints: `type(value)` gives the type itself. You want its name as text.
`type(value).__name__` is the name and `repr(value)` is the text form. Join them with `": "`.
`return type(value).__name__ + ": " + repr(value)`, and `return b, a` for the swap.
lessons.explanation:
`repr` is the form meant for programmers, so `"hi"` keeps its quotes and is easy to tell apart from the number or name it might look like.

`return b, a` builds a tuple. Commas make tuples, not parentheses. The same mechanism on the left side of `=` is what makes `x, y = y, x` work.

lessons.title: Printing output
lessons.body:
# Printing output

`print` takes any number of values, turns each one into text with `str`, and writes them with a space between and a newline at the end. Two keyword arguments change that.

```python
print("a", 1, True)       # a 1 True
print("a", "b", sep="-")  # a-b
print("same", end="")
print(" line")            # same line
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(*nums, sep=", ")    # 1, 2, 3
print()                   # empty line
```

- `sep` goes between the values. The default is one space.
- `end` goes after the last value. The default is `"\n"`, a newline.
- `*nums` spreads a list into separate arguments, so each item is printed on its own terms.

## Printing is not returning

`print` shows text to a person and gives back `None`. A function that works something out should usually `return` the result and let the caller decide whether to print it. Code that only prints is hard to reuse and hard to test.
lessons.task: Write `print_row(values)` that prints the values on one line separated by `" | "`. Write `print_list(words)` that prints the words on one line separated by `", "`, ending with `".\n"` instead of a plain newline.

out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    print_row([1, "a", 2.5])
text = out.getvalue()
assert text == '1 | a | 2.5\n', repr(text)

import contextlib, io
out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    print_row(["solo"])
text = out.getvalue()
assert text == 'solo\n', repr(text)

import contextlib, io
out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    a = print_row([1])
    b = print_list(["x"])
assert a is None and b is None, (a, b)

checks.name: prints a sentence
checks.code:
import contextlib, io
out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    print_list(["tea", "milk", "jam"])
text = out.getvalue()
assert text == 'tea, milk, jam.\n', repr(text)

checks.name: each call ends its own line
checks.code:
import contextlib, io
out = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
    print_list(["a"])
    print_list(["b", "c"])
text = out.getvalue()

hints: `print` already knows how to put text between several values. A list, though, is a single value.
`print(*values)` passes each item as its own argument, and `sep` sets what goes between them. `end` replaces the newline.
`print(*values, sep=" | ")`, and `print(*words, sep=", ", end=".\n")`.
lessons.explanation:
`print(values)` passes one argument, the list itself, so you see its brackets and the quotes around `'a'`. With `print(*values)` every item becomes its own argument, and `print` turns each one into text with `str`, which has no quotes.

`end` replaces the newline instead of adding to it. That is why the full stop version still has to include `\n`, or the next print would continue on the same line.

lessons.title: Strings and f-strings
lessons.body:
# Strings and f-strings

A string is an immutable sequence of characters. Methods return new strings and leave the original alone.

- `s.strip()` removes surrounding whitespace.
- `s.split()` breaks on any run of whitespace and returns a list.
- `"-".join(parts)` glues a list back together.
- `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` and `s[0]` do what they look like.

## f-strings

Put `f` before the quote and expressions inside braces. After a colon you can add a format spec.

```python
name = "Ada"
cost = 3.5
print(f"{name}: {cost:.2f}")
print(f"[{name:<6}]")   # [Ada   ]
print(f"[{cost:>6.2f}]")  # [  3.50]
print(f"{cost = }")     # cost = 3.5
```

`<` pads on the right, `>` pads on the left, and the number is the minimum width. Text longer than the width is not cut.

Python 3.14 also adds t-strings, a template form aimed at libraries. For everyday text, f-strings are the tool.

checks.code:
got = receipt_line("Tea", 3.5, 2)
assert got == "Tea        x2    7.00", repr(got)

checks.name: long names are not cut
checks.code:
got = receipt_line("Cappuccino grande", 4, 1)
assert got == "Cappuccino grande x1    4.00", repr(got)

checks.name: large totals still fit
checks.code:

assert got == "Desk       x3 3703.50", repr(got)

checks.name: initials
checks.code: assert initials("ada lovelace") == "AL", initials("ada lovelace")

checks.name: extra spaces and empty names
checks.code:
assert initials("  grace   brewster hopper ") == "GBH", initials("  grace   brewster hopper ")
assert initials("") == "", initials("")

hints: Each part of the line maps to one format spec: `<10` for the name and `>7.2f` for the total.
`split()` with no argument ignores extra whitespace, so empty words never appear in `initials`.
`f"{name:<10} x{qty} {total:>7.2f}"` for the line, and `"".join(w[0].upper() for w in full_name.split())` for the initials.
lessons.explanation:
Format specs keep layout in one place instead of counting spaces by hand. The width is a minimum, which is why a long name pushes the rest of the line right instead of being cut.

`split()` with no argument treats any run of whitespace as one separator, so `w[0]` is always safe. `split(" ")` would produce empty strings for double spaces, and `w[0]` would then raise `IndexError`.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.body:
# Numbers

`int` has no size limit. `float` is a 64-bit binary fraction, so most decimals are stored only approximately.

```python
print(7 / 2)    # 3.5, always a float
print(7 // 2)   # 3
print(-7 // 2)  # -4, rounds down
print(7 % 2)    # 1
print(2 ** 100) # exact, however large
print(divmod(7, 2))  # (3, 1)
```

## Comparing floats

```python
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # False
import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))  # True
```

`math.isclose` compares relative to the size of the numbers. Near zero that fails, because nothing is close relative to zero, so pass `abs_tol` too.

`round` sends exact halves to the nearest even number: `round(2.5)` is `2` and `round(3.5)` is `4`. For money, count whole cents in an `int` or use `decimal.Decimal`.
lessons.task: Write `split_bill(total_cents, people)` returning `(share, left_over)` in whole cents. Write `almost_equal(a, b)` using `math.isclose` with `abs_tol=1e-9`.

checks.name: splits with a remainder
checks.code: assert split_bill(1000, 3) == (333, 1), split_bill(1000, 3)

checks.name: even split leaves nothing
checks.code: assert split_bill(900, 3) == (300, 0), split_bill(900, 3)

checks.name: shares are whole numbers
checks.code:
share, left = split_bill(5, 10)
assert (share, left) == (0, 5), (share, left)
assert isinstance(share, int), type(share)

checks.name: float noise is ignored
checks.code:
assert almost_equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3), "0.1 + 0.2 should count as 0.3"
assert not almost_equal(1.0, 1.1), "1.0 and 1.1 are different"

checks.name: works near zero
checks.code: assert almost_equal(1e-12, 0.0), "needs abs_tol to work near zero"

hints: You want two results from one division. Python has a builtin for exactly that.
`/` always gives a float. `//` and `%` keep whole numbers, and `divmod` returns both at once.
`return divmod(total_cents, people)`, and `return math.isclose(a, b, abs_tol=1e-9)`.
lessons.explanation:
`divmod(a, b)` returns `(a // b, a % b)`. Keeping money in integer cents means no result is ever approximate.

`isclose` defaults to a relative tolerance of `1e-09`. Relative to zero, that tolerance is zero, so `isclose(1e-12, 0.0)` is false without `abs_tol`.

lessons.title: Comparisons and booleans
lessons.body:
# Comparisons and booleans

A comparison produces a `bool`, which is either `True` or `False`. A bool is an ordinary value: you can store it in a name, return it or print it.

```python
age = 17
is_adult = age >= 18
print(is_adult)            # False
print(3 == 3.0, 3 != 4)    # True True
print("apple" < "banana")  # True
print("Zebra" < "apple")   # True
print(True + True)         # 2
print(sum([True, False, True]))  # 2
```

- `==` and `!=` test equality. `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` test order.
- Strings compare character by character, by code point, so every capital letter sorts before every lowercase one. Compare `a.lower()` with `b.lower()` when case should not matter.
- `bool` is a kind of `int`: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` over bools counts the true ones.
- `1 < "2"` raises `TypeError`, while `1 == "1"` is simply `False`.

## Return the comparison

`return x > 0` already is `True` or `False`. Wrapping it in an `if` that returns `True` or `False` adds lines and room for mistakes.
lessons.task: Write `is_teen(age)` returning `True` for ages 13 to 19 inclusive and `False` otherwise. Write `count_passing(scores, pass_mark)` returning how many scores are at least `pass_mark`.

checks.name: teen ages, ends included
checks.code:
for age in [13, 15, 19]:
    assert is_teen(age) is True, (age, is_teen(age))

checks.name: other ages give False, not None
checks.code:
for age in [0, 12, 20, 45]:
    assert is_teen(age) is False, (age, is_teen(age))

checks.name: counts passing scores
checks.code: assert count_passing([40, 55, 70, 90], 55) == 3, count_passing([40, 55, 70, 90], 55)

checks.name: the mark itself passes
checks.code: assert count_passing([50, 50, 49], 50) == 2, count_passing([50, 50, 49], 50)

checks.name: no scores
checks.code:
got = count_passing([], 50)
assert got == 0, got
assert isinstance(got, int), type(got)

hints: A function that ends without `return` gives back `None`, which is not the same as `False`.
`13 <= age <= 19` is already a bool, so you can return it directly. For counting, each `score >= pass_mark` is `True` or `False`.
`return 13 <= age <= 19`, and `return sum(score >= pass_mark for score in scores)`.
lessons.explanation:
The first attempt has two problems: `>` and `<` leave out 13 and 19, and when the condition is false the function falls off the end and returns `None`. Returning the comparison itself fixes both, because it always produces a real `True` or `False`.

Since `True` is 1 and `False` is 0, `sum` over a run of comparisons counts how many were true. It reads as "add one for every passing score".

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.body:
# Branching

`if`, `elif` and `else` run the first block whose condition is true. Indentation marks the block.

```python
def label(n):
    if n < 0:
        return "negative"
    elif n == 0:
        return "zero"
    else:
        return "positive"
```

## Truthiness

Any value can be a condition. These count as false: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `None` and `False`. Almost everything else is true.

## Combining conditions

- `and`, `or` and `not` combine conditions and stop as soon as the answer is known.
- Comparisons chain: `0 < x <= 10` means `0 < x and x <= 10`.
- `a if condition else b` is an expression, handy for short choices.

Conditions are checked from top to bottom. Order them so that an earlier test does not swallow a case meant for a later one. Boundaries are where most branching bugs live, so test them first.
lessons.task: Write `shipping_cost(weight_kg, express=False)`: 0 for weight 0 or less, 5 up to and including 1 kg, 9 up to and including 5 kg, 15 above that, and express doubles the price. Write `is_leap(year)` for the Gregorian rule: divisible by 4, except centuries, unless divisible by 400.

checks.name: price bands
checks.code:
for weight, want in [(0.5, 5), (3, 9), (10, 15)]:
    assert shipping_cost(weight) == want, (weight, shipping_cost(weight))

checks.name: boundaries are inclusive
checks.code:
assert shipping_cost(1) == 5, shipping_cost(1)
assert shipping_cost(5) == 9, shipping_cost(5)

checks.name: nothing to ship
checks.code:
assert shipping_cost(0) == 0, shipping_cost(0)
assert shipping_cost(-2, express=True) == 0, shipping_cost(-2, express=True)

checks.name: express doubles
checks.code:
assert shipping_cost(1, express=True) == 10, shipping_cost(1, express=True)
assert shipping_cost(6, express=True) == 30, shipping_cost(6, express=True)

checks.name: leap years
checks.code:
assert is_leap(2024) and is_leap(2000), "2024 and 2000 are leap years"
assert not is_leap(2023) and not is_leap(1900), "2023 and 1900 are not"

hints: Handle the zero case first and return early, so the remaining branches only see real weights.
Pick the base price with `if`/`elif`/`else`, then apply express once at the end. For leap years, test the most specific rule first.
`if weight_kg <= 1: cost = 5`, `elif weight_kg <= 5: cost = 9`, `else: cost = 15`, then `return cost * 2 if express else cost`. For leap years test `% 400`, then `% 100`, then `% 4`.
lessons.explanation:
Returning early for the special case keeps the main logic flat. Each `elif` only runs when earlier conditions were false, so `weight_kg <= 5` already implies the weight is over 1.

The leap rule reads most clearly from the narrowest case outward: 400 wins over 100, and 100 wins over 4.

lessons.title: None, the missing value
lessons.body:
# None, the missing value

`None` is Python's value for "nothing here". A function that ends without `return` gives back `None`, and so does `print`.

```python
def find_user(name):
    if name == "ada":
        return "Ada Lovelace"

user = find_user("bob")
if user is None:
    print("not found")
result = print("hi")
print(result)  # None
```

There is only one `None` object, so test for it with `x is None` and `x is not None`, not with `==`.

## The trap with or

`x or default` gives `default` whenever `x` is false. That covers `None`, but also `0`, `""` and `[]`, which are often real answers:

```python
count = 0
print(count or 10)  # 10, wrong
if count is None:
    count = 10
print(count)        # 0, right
```

Use `None` to mean "not given" or "not found", and check it with `is None`. Then a zero, an empty string or an empty list stays what it is.
lessons.task: Write `describe_score(score)` returning `"no score"` when `score` is `None` and `f"score: {score}"` otherwise, where 0 is a real score. Write `pick(value, default)` returning `default` only when `value` is `None`, and `value` otherwise.

checks.name: missing score
checks.code: assert describe_score(None) == "no score", describe_score(None)

checks.name: zero is a real score
checks.code: assert describe_score(0) == "score: 0", describe_score(0)

checks.name: other scores
checks.code: assert describe_score(7) == "score: 7", describe_score(7)

checks.name: pick replaces None
checks.code:
assert pick(None, 5) == 5, pick(None, 5)
assert pick(3, 5) == 3, pick(3, 5)

checks.name: pick keeps false values
checks.code:
assert pick(0, 5) == 0, pick(0, 5)
assert pick("", "x") == "", pick("", "x")
assert pick([], [1]) == [], pick([], [1])

hints: `not score` is true for `None`, but also for `0`. You need a test that only `None` passes.
`value is None` is true for `None` and nothing else. Use it instead of truthiness in both functions.
`if score is None: return "no score"`, and in `pick`: `if value is None: return default`, then `return value`.
lessons.explanation:
Truthiness lumps `None` together with `0`, `""` and `[]`. That is handy when all of them mean "nothing", and wrong when zero is a valid score or an empty list is a valid answer.

`is None` asks exactly one question: was a value given at all? Use it whenever `None` stands for "missing", and the other false values keep their meaning.

lessons.title: Indexing and slicing
lessons.body:
# Indexing and slicing

Strings, lists and tuples are sequences. Each item has a position counted from 0, and negative positions count back from the end.

```python
word = "python"
print(word[0], word[-1])  # p n
print(word[1:4])   # yth
print(word[:2])    # py
print(word[2:])    # thon
print(word[-3:])   # hon
print(word[::2])   # pto
print(word[::-1])  # nohtyp
```

## How a slice reads

`s[start:stop:step]` begins at `start` and stops before `stop`, so `s[1:4]` holds 4 - 1 = 3 items. Leave out `start` to begin at the edge, `stop` to run to the other edge, and `step` to take every item. A negative step walks backwards.

- An index past the end raises `IndexError`.
- A slice past the end returns whatever exists, possibly an empty string.
- `s[:n]` is the first `n` items and `s[-n:]` the last `n`.
- A slice is a new object. Strings cannot be changed in place, so you build a new one instead.

keeps the length
checks.code: assert len(mask("abcdefgh")) == 8, mask("abcdefgh")

checks.name: short text is unchanged
checks.code:
for text in ["", "123", "1234"]:
    assert mask(text) == text, (text, mask(text))

checks.name: palindromes, any case
checks.code:

assert is_palindrome("Racecar") is True, is_palindrome("Racecar")

checks.name: other words

hints: The last four characters are a slice with a negative start. The rest is a count of `#` characters.
`"#" * n` repeats a string, and a negative `n` gives `""`. For the palindrome, lower-case the word before comparing it with its reverse.
`return "#" * (len(text) - 4) + text[-4:]`, and `word = word.lower()` then `return word == word[::-1]`.
lessons.explanation:
`text[-4:]` never raises: for text shorter than four characters it is the whole text. And `"#" * n` with `n` zero or negative is the empty string. Together they handle short input with no `if` at all.

`word[::-1]` is a reversed copy. Comparing `"Racecar"` with `"racecaR"` fails because `R` and `r` are different characters, so normalise the case first.

lessons.title: String methods
lessons.body:
# String methods

Strings have many methods, and none of them change the string. Each returns a new value, so keep the result.

```python
s = "  Hello, World  "
t = s.strip()
print(t.lower())             # hello, world
print(t.replace("World", "Ada"))
print(t.startswith("Hell"))  # True
print(t.find("o"), t.count("o"))  # 4 2
print("42".isdigit(), "4a".isdigit())
print("x" in t)              # False
print("k=v=w".partition("="))
```

- `find` returns the position of the first match, or -1. `index` does the same but raises `ValueError` when nothing matches.
- `count` counts matches that do not overlap.
- `isdigit`, `isalpha` and `isspace` are true only when every character fits.
- `split(",")` splits at every comma and keeps empty pieces.
- `partition("=")` splits once, at the first match, and returns three parts: before, the separator, after. If there is no match, the last two are empty.

A line like `s.upper()` on its own does nothing useful. Write `s = s.upper()`.
lessons.task: Write `parse_setting(line)` that turns text like `" Volume = 7 "` into `("volume", "7")`: split at the first `=`, strip both parts, lower-case the key, and return `None` if there is no `=`. Write `digits_only(text)` returning just the digit characters of `text`.

checks.name: strips and lower-cases
checks.code:
got = parse_setting(" Volume = 7 ")
assert got == ("volume", "7"), got

checks.name: splits at the first = only
checks.code:
got = parse_setting("url = a=b")
assert got == ("url", "a=b"), got

checks.name: no = gives None
checks.code: assert parse_setting("volume 7") is None, parse_setting("volume 7")

checks.name: keeps only digits
checks.code:

assert got == "15551234567", got

checks.name: no digits at all
checks.code: assert digits_only("call me") == "", digits_only("call me")

hints: `split("=")` splits at every `=`, so a value that contains `=` breaks the unpacking. One method splits only once.
`line.partition("=")` returns `(before, sep, after)`, and `sep` is empty when there was no `=`. For the digits, test each character with `isdigit`.
`key, sep, value = line.partition("=")`, return `None` if not `sep`, else `key.strip().lower(), value.strip()`. Then `"".join(ch for ch in text if ch.isdigit())`.
lessons.explanation:
`split("=")` gives three pieces for `"url = a=b"`, and unpacking three pieces into two names raises `ValueError`. `partition` always returns exactly three parts and tells you, through the middle one, whether the separator was there.

Removing the characters you expect, such as `-`, misses the ones you did not expect: spaces, brackets, a plus sign. Keeping only what you want is the safer direction.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.body:
# Loops

`for` walks over anything iterable. `while` repeats as long as a condition holds.

```python
for i in range(3):
    print(i)        # 0, 1, 2

names = ["a", "b"]
for i, n in enumerate(names):
    print(i, n)     # 0 a, then 1 b

for x, y in zip([1, 2], [3, 4]):
    print(x + y)    # 4, then 6
```

- `range(stop)` stops before `stop`. `range(start, stop, step)` also works, including negative steps.
- `enumerate` gives you the position without index arithmetic.
- `zip` stops at the shortest input.
- `break` leaves the loop. `continue` skips to the next pass.

Prefer `for` when you know what you are walking over. Use `while` when you only know when to stop:

```python
n = 40
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
print(n)  # 1
```
lessons.task: Write `collatz_steps(n)`: repeatedly halve even numbers and turn odd `n` into `3 * n + 1`, returning how many steps it takes to reach 1. Write `first_negative_index(numbers)` returning the index of the first negative number, or -1 if there is none.

checks.name: already at one
checks.code: assert collatz_steps(1) == 0, collatz_steps(1)

checks.name: counts steps
checks.code:
assert collatz_steps(6) == 8, collatz_steps(6)
assert collatz_steps(27) == 111, collatz_steps(27)

lessons.body:
# break, continue and else

Inside any loop, `break` leaves the loop at once and `continue` skips the rest of the current pass. A loop can also end with an `else` block, which runs only if the loop finished without a `break`.

```python
for n in [4, 9, 15, 21]:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        continue          # skip evens
    if n > 10:
        print("stopped at", n)
        break
    print("odd", n)
else:
    print("not printed: break ran")
```

## while True

When the exit test belongs in the middle of the loop, write `while True` and leave with `break`:

```python
total = 0
while True:
    total += 7
    if total > 30:
        break
print(total)  # 35
```

Read `else` on a loop as "no break happened". It fits searches: `break` when you find what you want, and put the not-found case in `else`. Keep loops short, so every `break` is easy to spot.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.body:
# Functions

`def` creates a function. Without a `return`, it returns `None`.

```python
def greet(name, greeting="Hi"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}"

greet("Ada")
greet("Ada", greeting="Hello")
```

## Parameter kinds

- A parameter with `=` has a default and may be left out.
- `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
- Anything after `*args` can only be passed by name. Those are keyword-only parameters.
- `**kwargs` collects extra named arguments into a dict.

```python
def log(*parts, sep=" "):
    return sep.join(parts)

log("a", "b")           # "a b"
log("a", "b", sep="-")  # "a-b"
```

Names assigned inside a function are local to it. A default value is computed once, when `def` runs, so never use a list or dict as a default. Use `None` and create the list inside.

lessons.title: Local and global scope
lessons.body:
# Local and global scope

A name assigned inside a function is local: it exists only while that call runs, and code outside cannot see it. To look a name up, Python checks the local scope, then any enclosing function, then the module level (global), then the builtins.

```python
rate = 2  # global

def scale(x):
    result = x * rate  # reads the global
    return result

print(scale(5))  # 10
print("result" in globals())  # False
```

## Assigning makes a name local

If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, that name is local for the whole function. So `count += 1` on a global raises `UnboundLocalError`, unless the function declares `global count` first.

```python
count = 0

def bump():
    global count
    count += 1

bump()
print(count)  # 1
```

`global` works, but a function that changes globals gives different answers depending on what ran before it. Pass values in as arguments and hand results back with `return`. And do not name your variables `sum`, `max` or `list`: that hides the builtin.

With a global, the second `tally([5])` returns 10, because the first call's points are still there. Nothing in the call itself tells you that, which is what makes global state hard to test.

When every value a function needs comes in as an argument and every result goes out through `return`, the same call always gives the same answer, wherever and however often it runs.

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.body:
# Lists

A list is an ordered, mutable sequence.

```python
xs = [30, 10, 20]
xs.append(40)
print(xs[0], xs[-1])  # 30 40
print(xs[1:3])        # [10, 20]
print(xs[::-1])       # reversed copy
```

Slices never raise for out-of-range bounds. They return whatever exists, and they build a new list.

## Sort in place or make a copy

- `xs.sort()` changes the list and returns `None`.
- `sorted(xs)` returns a new list and leaves `xs` alone.
- Both accept `reverse=True` and `key=len` style functions.

Do not change a list passed to you unless that is the function's stated job. The caller may still need it.

## Comprehensions

A comprehension builds a list from a loop in one expression:

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
big = [n * 10 for n in nums if n > 2]
print(big)  # [30, 40]
```

top_three(scores)
assert scores == [1, 3, 2, 5], scores

assert chunks([1, 2], 5) == [[1, 2]], chunks([1, 2], 5)

For `chunks`, `range` takes a step. `range(0, len(items), size)` gives the start of every chunk.
`return sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3]`, and `[items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]`.

`sorted` is `O(n log n)` and leaves the caller's list untouched. The slice handles short input with no special case.

The range step in `chunks` gives each start position once. The final slice may be short, and an empty input produces no starts at all, so the empty case needs no extra code.

lessons.title: List methods and copies
lessons.body:
# List methods and copies

Lists change in place. These methods modify the list and return `None`, except `pop`, which returns what it removed.

```python
xs = [3, 1]
xs.append(4)       # [3, 1, 4]
xs.extend([1, 5])  # [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
xs.insert(0, 9)    # [9, 3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
xs.remove(1)       # first 1 only
last = xs.pop()    # takes the 5
print(xs, last)    # [9, 3, 4, 1] 5
print(xs.index(4), xs.count(1))  # 2 1
```

`remove` and `index` raise `ValueError` when the value is not there, so check with `in` first. `pop(0)` takes from the front.

## Copies

`b = a` gives the same list a second name. `a.copy()`, `list(a)` and `a[:]` make a new outer list:

```python
a = [[1, 2], [3]]
b = a.copy()
b.append([4])
b[0].append(99)
print(a)  # [[1, 2, 99], [3]]
```

The copy is shallow: it holds the same inner lists. `copy.deepcopy` copies all the way down. `[[0] * 3] * 3` has the same trap, three references to one row.

lessons.title: Tuples and unpacking
lessons.body:
# Tuples and unpacking

A tuple is an ordered sequence that cannot change after it is made. Use one for a fixed group of values, such as a point or a record, and a list for a collection that grows.

```python
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point            # unpacking
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(x, y, first, rest)  # 3 4 1 [2, 3, 4]
single = (5,)           # the comma makes it
print(type(single).__name__)  # tuple
print((1, 2) == [1, 2])       # False
```

- Unpacking needs as many names as there are items, unless one name has a star, which collects the rest into a list.
- A function returns several values by returning a tuple, and the caller unpacks it.
- A tuple and a list with the same items are not equal.
- Tuples can be dict keys and set members, because they cannot change. Lists cannot.

```python
grid = {(0, 0): "start", (2, 1): "goal"}
for (row, col), name in grid.items():
    print(row, col, name)
```

`return min(numbers), max(numbers)`. In `walk`: `x, y = 0, 0`, `for dx, dy in steps: x, y = x + dx, y + dy`, then `return x, y`.

Commas make tuples, so `return min(numbers), max(numbers)` already returns one. A list was the wrong shape here: the result is a fixed pair, and `[1, 9] == (1, 9)` is `False`.

The starter `walk` replaced the position with each step instead of adding it. Unpacking the step in the `for` line names both parts, and the right side of `x, y = x + dx, y + dy` is computed in full before either name changes.

lessons.title: Dicts and sets
lessons.body:
# Dicts and sets

A dict maps keys to values. Lookup by key takes about the same time however large the dict is. Dicts keep insertion order.

```python
ages = {"ada": 36}
ages["alan"] = 41
print(ages.get("bob", 0))  # 0, no error
print("ada" in ages)       # True
for k, v in ages.items():
    print(k, v)
```

`d[key]` raises `KeyError` when the key is missing. `d.get(key, default)` does not. Keys must be hashable, so strings, numbers and tuples work and lists do not.

## Sets

A set holds unique values with no useful order, and it supports membership tests and set algebra.

```python
a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {2, 3, 4}
print(a & b)  # intersection
print(a | b)  # union
print(a - b)  # difference
```

Because a set's order is not guaranteed, sort it before showing or comparing it. Write `set()` for an empty set, since `{}` is an empty dict.

lessons.body:
# More comprehensions

The comprehension shape works for dicts and sets too, and it can choose a value for each item instead of filtering.

```python
words = ["tea", "milk", "tea", "jam"]
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words}
firsts = {w[0] for w in words}
sizes = ["big" if len(w) > 3 else "small"
         for w in words]
print(lengths)
print(sorted(firsts))  # ['j', 'm', 't']
print(sizes)
```

- A trailing `if` filters: items that fail it are left out.
- `a if condition else b` before the `for` picks a value for every item, so the result has one entry per input.
- Two `for` clauses run like nested loops, outer first: `[(r, c) for r in range(2) for c in range(3)]`.
- Round brackets give a generator expression, which feeds `sum`, `any`, `all`, `min` and `max` without building a list.

```python
nums = [3, 8, 12]
print(any(n > 10 for n in nums))  # True
print(all(n > 0 for n in nums))   # True
```

When a comprehension needs several conditions and a nested loop, a plain `for` loop is easier to read.

lessons.title: Grouping and counting
lessons.body:
# Grouping and counting

Two dict patterns come up again and again: counting how often each thing appears, and grouping items under a shared key.

```python
from collections import Counter

words = ["ant", "bee", "ape", "bat", "ant"]
counts = Counter(words)
print(counts["ant"], counts["cow"])  # 2 0
print(counts.most_common(1))  # [('ant', 2)]

groups = {}
for w in words:
    groups.setdefault(w[0], []).append(w)
print(groups)
```

- `Counter` is a dict that counts. A missing key reads as 0 instead of raising `KeyError`.
- `most_common(n)` returns the `n` biggest counts as `(item, count)` pairs, largest first. Equal counts keep the order in which the items were first seen.
- `d.setdefault(key, [])` returns the list stored under `key`, creating an empty one first if needed, so one line both creates and appends.
- `collections.defaultdict(list)` does the same job: a missing key gets a fresh empty list.

Each group keeps the order its items arrived in, which is usually what a reader expects.

assert got == {2: ["ox", "be"], 3: ["cat", "dog"]}, got

assert got == [("z", 1)], got

assert top_letters("", 3) == [], top_letters("", 3)

`groups.setdefault(len(word), [])` gives the existing list or a new one. For letters, lower-case the text and keep only characters where `isalpha()` is true.
`groups.setdefault(len(word), []).append(word)`, and `Counter([ch for ch in text.lower() if ch.isalpha()]).most_common(n)`.

Assigning `[word]` throws away the words collected so far for that length. `setdefault` creates the list only the first time and returns the same list on every later call, so `append` grows it.

`Counter(text)` counts every character, so spaces, `B` and `b` all get their own entries. Cleaning the input before counting keeps the counting code simple.

# Nested data

Real data is usually nested: a list of records, where each record is a dict that may hold lists of its own. Read it one layer at a time.

```python

print(orders[0]["items"][1])  # jam
```

- Use `record.get("key", default)` when some records may lack a field.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.body:
# Recursion

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller piece of the problem. It needs a base case that it answers directly, and every other call must move closer to that base case.

```python
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:          # base case
        return ["go"]
    return [n] + countdown(n - 1)

print(countdown(3))  # [3, 2, 1, 'go']
```

Recursion suits data that is shaped like itself, such as lists that contain lists:

```python
def count_items(data):
    total = 0
    for x in data:
        if isinstance(x, list):
            total += count_items(x)
        else:
            total += 1
    return total

print(count_items([1, [2, [3]], 4]))  # 4
```

`isinstance(x, list)` asks whether `x` is a list. Each inner list is handled by the same function, however deep it sits. Python stops runaway recursion after about 1000 nested calls with `RecursionError`, so for a long, flat sequence a loop is the better tool.

    assert depth(data) == want, (data, depth(data))

assert got == 3, got
assert depth([[[[]]]]) == 4, depth([[[[]]]])

In `nested_sum`, `total += nested_sum(x)` for lists and `total += x` otherwise. In `depth`, `deepest = max(deepest, depth(x))` for lists, then `return 1 + deepest`.

The base case here is hidden in the loop: a list with no inner lists makes no further calls. An empty list returns 0 for the sum and 1 for the depth, so empty lists at any level need no special handling.

lessons.title: Sorting with key and lambda
lessons.body:
# Sorting with key and lambda

`sorted`, `min` and `max` accept `key`: a function applied to each item, whose result is compared instead of the item itself.

```python
words = ["kiwi", "Fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words))          # Fig first
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))
print(max(words, key=len))    # banana

people = [("ada", 36), ("alan", 41)]
oldest = max(people, key=lambda p: p[1])
print(oldest)  # ('alan', 41)
```

`lambda args: expression` makes a small unnamed function. Use it where a function is needed only once.

## Several keys

Return a tuple to sort by more than one thing. Tuples compare item by item, so `key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])` sorts by age, oldest first, and then by name. The minus sign reverses only the number. Sorting is stable: items with equal keys keep their original order.

`min` and `max` return the first of several equal items, and take `default=` for an empty input. `map(f, xs)` and `filter(f, xs)` apply or test a function on each item, though a comprehension usually reads better.

`max(words)` compares the words themselves, alphabetically. `key=len` compares lengths instead, and because `max` keeps the first of equal items, ties go to the earlier word. Without `default`, an empty list raises `ValueError`.

lessons.title: Errors and try/except
lessons.body:
# Errors and try/except

An exception stops normal flow and travels up the call stack until something handles it.

```python
def to_int(text):
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError:
        return None
```

- `try` holds the code that might fail.
- `except SomeError` handles only that type, and its subclasses.
- `else` runs if nothing was raised.
- `finally` always runs, which suits cleanup.

## Catch what you expect

A bare `except:` or a wide `except Exception:` also hides your own bugs. Name the exact error you know how to handle and let the rest propagate.

## Raising

```python
def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"bad age: {age}")
    return age
```

Use `except (ValueError, TypeError):` for several types at once. Python 3.14 also accepts that without the parentheses, when there is no `as` clause.

lessons.title: Raising your own exceptions
lessons.body:
# Raising your own exceptions

When a function cannot do its job, `raise` an exception rather than returning an odd value that the caller might not check. Pick the built-in type that fits: `ValueError` for a bad value, `TypeError` for a wrong type, `KeyError` for a missing key.

For errors that belong to your program, define your own class. It only needs a name and a parent:

```python
class OutOfStock(Exception):
    pass

def take(stock, item):
    if stock.get(item, 0) == 0:
        raise OutOfStock(f"no {item} left")
    stock[item] -= 1

try:
    take({"tea": 0}, "tea")
except OutOfStock as error:
    print("sorry:", error)
```

- `except SomeError as error` gives you the exception object, and `str(error)` is its message.
- Inherit from `ValueError` or `LookupError` when your error is a special case of one, so handlers that already catch the parent keep working.
- Write messages that say what went wrong and with which values.

assert withdraw(5, 5) == 0, withdraw(5, 5)

checks.name: it is a ValueError
checks.code: assert issubclass(InsufficientFunds, ValueError), "InsufficientFunds should inherit from ValueError"

checks.name: too much raises InsufficientFunds
bad amounts raise a plain ValueError

hints: Returning `None` lets a caller carry on as if the money had been taken. Raising makes the problem impossible to miss.
Put `ValueError` in the brackets of the class line. Check the amount first, then the balance, and build each message with an f-string.
`class InsufficientFunds(ValueError): pass`, then `if amount <= 0: raise ValueError(...)` and `if amount > balance: raise InsufficientFunds(f"cannot take {amount} from {balance}")`.
lessons.explanation:
A `None` result is easy to ignore: `balance = withdraw(balance, 50)` quietly sets the balance to `None`. An exception stops the program at the exact point of the problem, unless the caller has decided how to handle it.

Making `InsufficientFunds` a `ValueError` gives callers a choice. They can catch the specific case and offer a smaller amount, or catch `ValueError` and treat every bad withdrawal the same way.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.body:
# Reading and writing files

`open` returns a file object. Use `with` so it closes even if an error happens.

```python
with open("notes.txt", "w",
          encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("first\n")

with open("notes.txt",
          encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip("\n"))
```

- Mode `"r"` reads and is the default. `"w"` replaces the file. `"a"` appends.
- Always pass `encoding="utf-8"`, so text behaves the same everywhere.
- Each line you iterate over keeps its newline. `write` adds none, so you add it yourself.
- Opening a missing file for reading raises `FileNotFoundError`.

## pathlib

`pathlib.Path` wraps a path in an object, with shortcuts for whole-file work:

```python
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("notes.txt")
p.write_text("hi\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(p.exists(), p.suffix)
```

lessons.title: Paths and folders
lessons.body:
# Paths and folders

`pathlib.Path` joins path parts with `/`, so the same code works on every system. A `Path` is only a name until you ask it to touch the disk.

```python
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("notes")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
a = folder / "a.txt"
a.write_text("hi", encoding="utf-8")
b = folder / "b.md"
b.write_text("yo", encoding="utf-8")

print(a.name, a.stem, a.suffix)
print(a.parent)  # notes
txt = folder.glob("*.txt")
print(sorted(p.name for p in txt))
```

- `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` creates any missing parent folders and does not fail when the folder already exists.
- `iterdir()` lists a folder's entries. `glob("*.txt")` matches names, and `rglob` also searches subfolders.
- `is_file()` and `is_dir()` tell entries apart, and `exists()` checks either.
- `a.with_suffix(".bak")` is a new path with another extension.

The order of `iterdir` and `glob` results is not defined, so sort them before you depend on it.

def save_note(folder, name, text):

    path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")

lessons.title: JSON files
lessons.body:
# JSON files

JSON is a text format for nested data that almost every language can read. The `json` module turns dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and `None` into JSON text and back.

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

data = {"name": "Ada", "langs": ["py"],
        "active": True, "boss": None}
p = Path("user.json")
with p.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

with p.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
print(loaded == data)  # True
```

- `dump` and `load` work with files. `dumps` and `loads`, with an s for string, work with text.
- `indent=2` makes the file readable, and `sort_keys=True` gives a stable key order.
- Tuples come back as lists, and dict keys always come back as strings.
- A `set` cannot be saved and raises `TypeError`. Convert it to a list first, and back again after loading.

A JSON file is a good fit for settings and small saved state. It is plain text, so you can open it and read it.

lessons.title: Dates and times
lessons.body:
# Dates and times

The `datetime` module has `date` for calendar days, `datetime` for a day plus a time of day, and `timedelta` for a length of time.

```python
from datetime import date, timedelta

d = date.fromisoformat("2024-02-27")
later = d + timedelta(days=3)
print(later)               # 2024-03-01
print((later - d).days)    # 3
print(later.strftime("%d %b %Y"))
print(later.weekday())     # 4, a Friday
print(later.isoformat() > "2024-01-31")
```

- `fromisoformat` reads, and `isoformat` writes, the `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Text in that form also sorts in date order.
- Adding a `timedelta` handles month ends and leap years for you. Subtracting two dates gives a `timedelta`, and `.days` is a whole number.
- `strftime` formats a date with codes such as `%Y`, `%m`, `%d` and `%A`, the weekday name. `strptime` parses text with the same codes.
- `weekday()` counts Monday as 0.

`date.today()` and `datetime.now()` change every day. Pass dates into your functions instead of reading the clock inside them, so the functions stay testable.

`date.fromisoformat(text)` turns the text into a date. Subtract two dates for a `timedelta`, or add `timedelta(days=days)` to move forward.
`(date.fromisoformat(end) - date.fromisoformat(start)).days`, and `(date.fromisoformat(start) + timedelta(days=days)).isoformat()`.
lessons.explanation:
Counting with the day of the month gives the right answer inside one month and nonsense across a boundary: February 30th, or 3 minus 27. Months of different lengths and leap years are exactly what `date` and `timedelta` already know.

Converting text to `date` objects at the edges, doing the work with dates, and converting back with `isoformat` keeps the calendar rules out of your own code.

lessons.title: math and random
lessons.body:
# math and random

The `math` module holds the usual functions for numbers, and `random` makes pseudo-random choices.

```python
import math

print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)
print(math.floor(2.7), math.ceil(2.1))
print(math.hypot(3, 4))      # 5.0
print(math.dist((0, 0), (1, 1)))
print(math.prod([2, 3, 4]))  # 24
```

`math.floor` rounds down and `math.ceil` rounds up, and both return an `int`. `math.dist` measures a straight line between two points.

## Seeded randomness

```python
import random

rng = random.Random(7)
print(rng.randint(1, 6))     # 1 to 6
print(rng.choice(["a", "b"]))
print(rng.random())          # below 1
```

A seed fixes the sequence: `random.Random(7)` makes the same choices on every run, which tests need. `randint(a, b)` includes both ends, unlike `range`. Make your own `Random` object instead of calling `random.seed`, which resets the generator that every other part of the program shares.
lessons.task: Write `roll_dice(n, seed)` returning a list of `n` six-sided die rolls made with its own `random.Random(seed)`, without touching the shared generator. Write `distance(a, b)` returning the straight-line distance between two `(x, y)` points.

checks.name: rolls are 1 to 6
checks.code:
rolls = roll_dice(50, 3)
assert len(rolls) == 50, len(rolls)
assert all(1 <= r <= 6 for r in rolls), rolls

checks.name: every face can appear
checks.code:
got = set(roll_dice(300, 5))
assert got == {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, sorted(got)

checks.name: a seed repeats its rolls
checks.code:
assert roll_dice(10, 42) == roll_dice(10, 42), "the same seed should give the same rolls"
assert roll_dice(20, 1) != roll_dice(20, 2), "different seeds should give different rolls"

checks.name: the shared generator is untouched
checks.code:
import random
random.seed(0)
want = random.random()
random.seed(0)
roll_dice(5, 1)
got = random.random()
assert got == want, "roll_dice changed the shared random generator"

checks.name: straight-line distance
checks.code:
assert distance((0, 0), (3, 4)) == 5.0, distance((0, 0), (3, 4))
assert distance((1, 1), (1, 1)) == 0.0, distance((1, 1), (1, 1))
assert abs(distance((-1, 0), (2, -4)) - 5.0) < 1e-9, distance((-1, 0), (2, -4))

hints: `random.seed` resets the generator every module shares. Your function should have a generator of its own.
`rng = random.Random(seed)` creates one, and `rng.randint(1, 6)` rolls it. For the distance, `math` has a function that takes two points.
`rng = random.Random(seed)`, then `[rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]`, and `return math.dist(a, b)`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter's rolls are repeatable, but it resets the shared generator as a side effect, so any other code using `random` suddenly gets a different sequence. A private `Random(seed)` gives the same repeatable rolls and leaves everything else alone.

Adding the differences is not a distance: it can even be negative. The straight line is the square root of the squared differences, which `math.dist` computes for points of any dimension.

lessons.title: Project: a word report
lessons.body:
# Project: a word report

This lesson puts the course together. A word report reads text, cleans it into words, counts them and lists the most common ones. Split the job into small functions so each step can be tested alone.

```python
import string
from collections import Counter

print(string.punctuation)
print("'Hi!'".strip(string.punctuation))
print("don't".strip(string.punctuation))
print(repr("...".strip(string.punctuation)))

words = ["the", "cat", "the"]
print(Counter(words).most_common(1))
```

## The plan

- `clean_words` lower-cases the text, splits it on whitespace, strips punctuation from both ends of each piece, and drops pieces that end up empty. Stripping only the ends keeps words like `don't` whole.
- `Counter(words).most_common(n)` finds the top words. Equal counts keep the order in which the words first appeared.
- Formatting comes last, in its own function, so the counting can be checked without reading printed text.

Test each function on a tiny input you can count by hand before trusting it with a long text.
lessons.task: Write `clean_words(text)` returning the lower-case words of `text`, with punctuation stripped from both ends of each and empty results dropped. Write `report(text, n)` returning the `n` most common words as lines like `"cat: 2"` joined with newlines, or `"no words"` when there are none.

checks.name: lower-cases and strips
checks.code:
got = clean_words("Hello, World!")
assert got == ["hello", "world"], got

checks.name: keeps inner apostrophes
checks.code:
got = clean_words("Don't stop -- ever.")
assert got == ["don't", "stop", "ever"], got
assert clean_words("  ... ") == [], clean_words("  ... ")

checks.name: reports the top words
checks.code:
got = report("The cat sat. The cat ran! the end", 2)
assert got == "the: 3\ncat: 2", repr(got)

checks.name: ties keep first appearance
checks.code:
got = report("b a b a c", 3)
assert got == "b: 2\na: 2\nc: 1", repr(got)

checks.name: nothing to report
checks.code: assert report("?! ...", 3) == "no words", report("?! ...", 3)

hints: `split` alone keeps capitals and the punctuation stuck to words, such as `"World!"`. Clean every piece before counting.
Loop over `text.lower().split()`, call `piece.strip(string.punctuation)` and keep the result only if it is not empty. In `report`, build one f-string per pair from `most_common(n)`.

In `clean_words`, append each non-empty `piece.strip(string.punctuation)`. In `report`, return `"no words"` for an empty `Counter`, else `"\n".join(f"{word}: {count}" for word, count in counts.most_common(n))`.
lessons.explanation:
Without cleaning, `"The"`, `"the"` and `"cat."` count as different words, and the report is quietly wrong. Normalising case and trimming punctuation first means every later step works on clean data, and `strip` only touches the ends, so `don't` survives.

`str(counts.most_common(n))` is a Python list printed as text, not a report a person wants to read. Keeping counting and formatting in separate steps means each one can be tested alone, which is how longer programs stay manageable.
